segments.title: Benchmark ships frame the ideal destroyer
segments.body: The opening distinction is between a useful benchmark and a claim that a particular ship was the best destroyer of its period. The pictures provide concrete examples for discussing each era. The standard is what an ideal destroyer needed at the time, rather than a ranking of individual classes. Starting here explains how to read the comparisons that follow.

evidence.note: The transcript says the pictures show benchmark destroyers for discussing the period's ideal rather than necessarily the best destroyers of their periods.

segments.summary: The ships shown are period benchmarks chosen to explain what an ideal destroyer required, not declarations that each pictured design was the best of its era.

segments.title: National roles shape destroyer design
segments.body: No destroyer is ideal in the abstract because its best features depend on the role a navy expects it to perform. A navy using destroyers chiefly as a shield may favour gun firepower, while one using them as a spear may stress torpedoes. A general-purpose design also needs anti-submarine and minelaying capability alongside guns and torpedoes. The same design can therefore suit one fleet and disappoint another because doctrine changes the value placed on each system. This passage frames destroyer design as a balance of operational priorities rather than a universal checklist.

evidence.note: Comparison of shield, spear, and general-purpose destroyer roles with their armament and capability priorities.

segments.summary: A destroyer optimized for fleet protection, offensive attack, or general-purpose duties will make different tradeoffs in guns, torpedoes, anti-submarine warfare, and minelaying.
